modules.title: SOLID & Object-Oriented Principles
modules.description: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion.

concepts.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
concepts.summary: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.

concepts.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
concepts.summary: Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.

concepts.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
concepts.summary: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering correctness.

concepts.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
concepts.summary: Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.

concepts.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
concepts.summary: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.

concepts.title: Composition Over Inheritance
concepts.summary: Favoring object composition over class inheritance to avoid fragile base class traps.

concepts.title: Law of Demeter (Least Knowledge)
concepts.summary: Objects should only talk to immediate friends, avoiding chained dereference coupling.

concepts.title: Encapsulation & Information Hiding
concepts.summary: Exposing minimal public surface area while keeping internal state representation private.

concepts.title: Design Smells: Rigidity, Fragility & Immobility
concepts.summary: Diagnosing code rot and architectural entropy before refactoring.

concepts.title: Inversion of Control (IoC) & Dependency Injection
concepts.summary: Decoupling object instantiation and lifecycle management from business execution.

theory.overview: SOLID principles represent the foundation of maintainable, extensible object-oriented design. They provide clear heuristics to avoid fragile, tightly coupled code that breaks whenever requirements change.
theory.whyItMatters: Violating SOLID creates rigid codebases where modifying a single class requires editing dozens of unrelated files across the project.
keyMechanisms: Depend on abstractions (interfaces), never concrete implementation classes.
Favor composition and delegation over class inheritance.
Enforce single responsibility to keep classes focused, cohesive, and easily testable.

whyTheseConcepts.design-principles-solid: Establishes architectural invariants and failure mitigation for design principles solid within solid & object-oriented principles.

modules.title: Creational Patterns & Object Lifecycle
modules.description: Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton, and lazy initialization.

concepts.title: Factory Method Pattern
concepts.summary: Defining an interface for creating an object, but letting subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

concepts.title: Abstract Factory Pattern
concepts.summary: Providing an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying concrete classes.

concepts.title: Builder Pattern with Fluent Interfaces
concepts.summary: Separating complex object construction from its representation, supporting step-by-step assembly.

concepts.title: Builder Validation & Invariant Enforcement
concepts.summary: Validating cross-field business constraints during build() before object instantiation.

concepts.title: Prototype Pattern & Deep Copying
concepts.summary: Specifying kinds of objects to create using a prototypical instance and cloning new objects.

concepts.title: Singleton Pattern & Thread Safety
concepts.summary: Ensuring a class has only one instance and providing a global point of access.

concepts.title: Double-Checked Locking & Volatile Semantics
concepts.summary: Thread-safe lazy initialization of singletons without synchronization performance overhead.

concepts.title: Object Pooling Pattern
concepts.summary: Reusing expensive objects (database connections, threads, socket buffers) to minimize GC allocation.

concepts.title: Dependency Injection Container Lifecycles
concepts.summary: Singleton, Scoped, and Transient dependency lifecycles in Spring and Guice.

concepts.title: Design a Thread-Safe Bounded Blocking Queue
concepts.summary: Implementing a thread-safe bounded queue with ReentrantLock and Condition variables.

theory.overview: Creational patterns abstract the instantiation process. They make systems independent of how their objects are created, composed, and represented, avoiding tight coupling to concrete constructors.
theory.whyItMatters: Spattering 'new ConcreteClass()' throughout application code makes unit testing with mocks impossible and locks the system into rigid implementations.
keyMechanisms: Builders guarantee that objects with complex parameters are never created in an invalid state.
Factories isolate object instantiation logic behind clean polymorphic interfaces.
Object pools reduce garbage collection overhead for high-frequency short-lived resources.

concepts.title: Adapter Pattern (Object vs Class Adapter)
concepts.summary: Converting the interface of a class into another interface clients expect.

concepts.title: Decorator Pattern for Dynamic Behavior
concepts.summary: Attaching additional responsibilities to an object dynamically without subclassing.

concepts.title: Java I/O Streams as Decorator Archetype
concepts.summary: BufferedInputStream wrapping FileInputStream: nested stream composition.

concepts.title: Proxy Pattern: Virtual, Protection & Dynamic Proxies
concepts.summary: Providing a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.

concepts.title: Dynamic Proxies & AOP Interceptors
concepts.summary: JDK Dynamic Proxies and CGLIB bytecode enhancement for transactional aspect-oriented programming.

concepts.title: Facade Pattern for Subsystem Simplification
concepts.summary: Providing a unified, simplified high-level interface to a complex subsystem of classes.

concepts.title: Composite Pattern for Tree Hierarchies
concepts.summary: Composing objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies uniformly.

concepts.title: Bridge Pattern: Decoupling Abstraction from Implementation
concepts.summary: Decoupling an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently.

concepts.title: Flyweight Pattern for Memory Optimization
concepts.summary: Sharing fine-grained object state to support large numbers of objects efficiently.

concepts.title: Implement an LRU Cache

theory.overview: Structural patterns ease the design by identifying a simple way to realize relationships among entities. They ensure that when one part of a system changes, the entire structure does not need to adapt.
theory.whyItMatters: Without structural adapters and facades, third-party libraries and legacy systems leak implementation details across all application layers.
keyMechanisms: Adapters enable incompatible interfaces to collaborate seamlessly.
Decorators adhere to Open/Closed by adding behavior dynamically without modifying existing classes.
Proxies transparently inject security checks, caching, and lazy loading.

concepts.title: Strategy Pattern vs Conditional Branching

concepts.title: Command Pattern: Encapsulating Invocations

concepts.title: Template Method Pattern: Inversion of Control

concepts.title: State Pattern: Finite State Machines
concepts.summary: Allowing an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes.

concepts.title: Chain of Responsibility Pattern

theory.overview: Behavioral patterns are concerned with algorithms and the assignment of responsibilities between objects. They characterize complex control flow that is difficult to follow at runtime.
theory.whyItMatters: Hardcoding algorithmic variations inside monolithic conditional branches creates brittle, untestable code prone to regression bugs.
keyMechanisms: Strategy isolates algorithmic variations behind a common polymorphic interface.
Command turns operations into first-class objects that can be queued, delayed, or reversed.
Chain of Responsibility enables dynamic, extensible request processing pipelines.

concepts.title: Mediator Pattern: Centralized Coordination
concepts.summary: Defining an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, preventing chaotic many-to-many references.

concepts.title: Mediator vs Observer in Event Systems
concepts.summary: Centralized hub coordination vs decentralized broadcast notification.

concepts.title: Iterator Pattern & Custom Collections

concepts.title: Memento Pattern: Capturing Internal State

theory.overview: Coordinating complex communication between multiple collaborating objects requires decoupling senders from receivers. Observer and Mediator patterns turn tight dependencies into clean event flows.
theory.whyItMatters: Direct many-to-many references between UI components or service classes produce tightly coupled systems where any change causes ripple effects.
keyMechanisms: Observer establishes one-to-many event notification without coupling subjects to concrete listeners.
Always pair Observer registration with explicit deregistration to prevent memory leaks.
Mediator centralizes complex interaction rules into a single coordinator class.

theory.overview: Concurrency patterns manage simultaneous execution safely. They prevent race conditions, deadlocks, and memory visibility bugs in multi-threaded environments.
theory.whyItMatters: Improper concurrent synchronization causes non-deterministic data corruption that cannot be caught by standard unit tests.
keyMechanisms: Producer-consumer queues decouple processing speeds and buffer microbursts safely.
Read-write locks maximize throughput for read-heavy workloads but risk writer starvation.
Always clean up ThreadLocal variables in thread pool environments to prevent memory leaks.

theory.overview: Enterprise Integration Patterns (EIP) standardize how heterogeneous distributed systems exchange data reliably over messaging backbones using proven integration idioms.
theory.whyItMatters: Custom ad-hoc integration logic between systems produces fragile, unmonitored point-to-point connections that break on schema changes.
keyMechanisms: Pipes and filters allow individual data transformation stages to scale and be tested independently.
Aggregators require correlation IDs and timeout handlers to prevent memory leaks from stranded incomplete batches.
Wire taps provide non-intrusive auditing and observability without impacting message flow.

theory.overview: Persistence patterns decouple domain business rules from underlying relational or NoSQL database schemas, ensuring data access is transactional, efficient, and testable.
theory.whyItMatters: The N+1 query problem is the #1 database performance killer in production applications using ORMs.
keyMechanisms: Unit of Work aggregates all database modifications into a single optimized batch flush.
Data Mapper keeps domain entities completely pure of database columns or SQL annotations.
Always check query logs for N+1 query loops when traversing object associations.

theory.overview: Cloud resilience patterns ensure applications survive transient network failures, service outages, and traffic surges gracefully without human intervention.
theory.whyItMatters: Cascading failures occur when a single degraded dependency exhausts thread pools across all upstream microservices.
keyMechanisms: Never retry without randomized jitter; synchronized retries act as self-inflicted DDoS attacks.
Always separate liveness checks (restart pod) from readiness checks (remove from traffic).
Circuit breakers provide degraded services the breathing room needed to recover.

Sidecars handle cross-cutting network concerns without polluting core business domain code.
Leader election ensures exactly one node coordinates cluster state transitions.

keyMechanisms: Refactor only under green tests: change behavior or change structure, never both simultaneously.
Introduce patterns as destinations to remove specific code smells, not as speculative upfront abstractions.
Modern languages replace many GoF patterns with native lambdas, immutability, and pattern matching.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: Design patterns are battle-tested structural, behavioral, and architectural idioms that decouple software components and resolve recurring system engineering challenges with loose coupling, high cohesion, and runtime resilience. They provide standardized blueprints for managing object lifecycles, isolating fault domains, executing distributed transactions, and guaranteeing idempotency across evolving codebases.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Writing ad-hoc procedural code without structured design idioms leads to rigid, fragile systems where a single requirement change ripples through hundreds of files. In production, unpatterned microservices cascade failures when downstream dependencies slow down, and dual-write operations cause silent data divergence. Mastering structural and resilience design patterns (Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads, Sagas, and Transactional Outbox) is essential for engineering reliable, testable software.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: Design patterns are not intellectual decorations to showcase complexity; they are surgical tools to isolate change, contain failure blast radius, and make distributed workflows recoverable.
coreArchitectureRules: Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software artifacts should be open for extension, but closed for modification. Extend behavior through polymorphism, composition, and strategy patterns rather than mutating stable core classes.

Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level business policies must not depend on low-level technical mechanisms (such as database drivers or HTTP clients). Both must depend on stable abstractions/interfaces.

Composition Over Inheritance: Prefer object composition (has-a relationships) over class inheritance (is-a relationships) to prevent fragile base class hierarchies and encourage flexible runtime behavior swapping.

Resilience Boundary Isolation: Every remote integration must be wrapped in a fault isolation pattern (Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, and Timeout) to prevent transient external outages from crashing the host application.

Transactional Atomicity (Dual-Write Prevention): Never execute a local database write and publish a message broker event in the same code block without a coordinating Transactional Outbox or 2PC pattern.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Inconsistency (Ghost Messages)
failureModes.description: An application writes an order to PostgreSQL and then immediately calls Kafka.send(). If the network drops or the pod crashes before Kafka acknowledges, the order exists in the DB but the event is never published.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement the Transactional Outbox Pattern: save the event into an outbox table within the same ACID database transaction, and tail the outbox asynchronously via Change Data Capture (Debezium).

failureModes.name: Thread Pool Starvation (Unbounded Bulkhead Failure)
failureModes.description: A third-party payment gateway slows down from 50ms to 12,000ms. All incoming application threads block waiting for payment responses, exhausting the shared web server thread pool and halting all other unrelated traffic.
failureModes.mitigation: Isolate external calls with dedicated thread/semaphore Bulkheads and strict 1000ms timeouts, failing fast when the concurrency threshold is breached.

failureModes.name: Circuit Breaker Rapid Flapping
failureModes.description: A circuit breaker transitions from Closed to Open and immediately back to Half-Open on the first success, oscillating repeatedly under flapping downstream conditions and blasting struggling backends.
failureModes.mitigation: Introduce hysteresis and progressive probe testing: require a sustained sequence of consecutive successful canary requests in Half-Open before fully closing the breaker.

failureModes.name: Saga Compensation Cascade Failure
failureModes.description: A distributed checkout saga encounters a failure at step 4, but compensating transactions at step 2 fail due to unhandled exceptions, leaving customer bank accounts debited with no order created.
failureModes.mitigation: Design every compensation step to be strictly idempotent, persistently retried with dead-letter queue escalation, and backed by automated reconciliation jobs.

whenToUse: When system requirements dictate loose coupling between business logic and infrastructure dependencies (storage, third-party APIs, messaging).
Distributed microservice architectures requiring resilient cross-service communications and graceful degradation during network hiccups.
Multi-step business workflows spanning multiple autonomous microservices that cannot use single-database ACID transactions.
Complex domain applications where algorithms or business rules vary dynamically based on customer tier, region, or runtime flags.
whenNotToUse: Trivial CRUD endpoints and internal script utilities where adding interfaces, factories, and strategies creates excessive boilerplate.
Speculative abstraction: creating factory patterns for classes that will only ever have exactly one concrete implementation for the foreseeable future.
Performance-critical inner execution loops where virtual dispatch, interface lookups, and heap allocations add unacceptable nanosecond latency overhead.
Scenarios where simpler functional composition (pure functions and higher-order functions) achieves the same outcome without object-oriented ceremony.

tradeOffs.pro: Sagas eliminate distributed lock contention across microservices, scaling horizontally without blocking database connections.
tradeOffs.con: Sagas require writing complex compensating rollback transactions and sacrifice immediate cross-service isolation (dirty reads are visible during execution).

tradeOffs.factor: Transactional Outbox with Polling vs Change Data Capture (CDC)
tradeOffs.pro: Polling an outbox table with SQL is simple to implement and requires zero external infrastructure changes.
tradeOffs.con: Polling creates database CPU overhead and latency lag; CDC (Debezium) operates at transaction log level with sub-millisecond lag but requires Kafka Connect infrastructure.

tradeOffs.factor: Circuit Breakers: Client-Side vs Mesh Sidecar (Envoy)
tradeOffs.pro: Mesh sidecars (Envoy/Istio) enforce circuit breakers transparently across polyglot microservices without code changes.
tradeOffs.con: Client-side libraries (Resilience4j) have semantic awareness of business exceptions, whereas network proxies only see generic HTTP 5xx codes.

productionScenarios.title: Zero-Data-Loss Financial Outbox at FinTech Unicorn
productionScenarios.scenario: A banking ledger occasionally lost withdrawal notifications when microservice pods were terminated during Kubernetes auto-scaling events right after DB commits.
productionScenarios.outcome: Implemented the Transactional Outbox pattern with Debezium CDC streaming Postgres write-ahead logs (WAL) to Kafka, guaranteeing exactly-once event publication and recovering $4.2M in uncollected merchant fees.

productionScenarios.title: Circuit Breaker Protection During Partner API Blackout
productionScenarios.scenario: An international airline booking portal collapsed during an airport partner API outage because 10,000 passenger requests blocked on unresponsive SOAP endpoints.
productionScenarios.outcome: Configured adaptive Circuit Breakers and Bulkhead pools. During partner failure, booking requests degraded gracefully by offering cached flight estimates with delayed ticketing, preserving 99.98% portal availability.

coreChallenges.title: Coupling vs Extensibility (SOLID Principles)
coreChallenges.explanation: Hardcoding concrete dependencies creates tight coupling that makes automated testing and feature swapping painful. Dependency inversion and composition over inheritance preserve flexibility.

coreChallenges.title: Fault Isolation & Resilience Patterns
coreChallenges.explanation: In microservices, a single failing dependency can exhaust thread pools. Circuit breakers, bulkheads, and timeouts isolate failures and enable graceful degradation.

coreChallenges.title: Distributed Transaction Coordination
coreChallenges.explanation: Two-phase commit is brittle in microservices. The Saga pattern coordinates distributed business transactions across multiple services using compensations and local transactions.

coreChallenges.title: Dual-Write Inconsistency & Outbox Pattern
coreChallenges.explanation: Writing to a database and publishing to a message broker in the same operation is non-atomic. The Transactional Outbox pattern guarantees atomic state commits and reliable event delivery.
